EPIDEMIC CONTEXT — Brazil declared a public health emergency for dengue in February 2024; case volumes for Q1 2024 are exceptionally high. Collectors should expect large cumulative figures and frequent situation report updates.
SEROTYPE CONTEXT — Multiple DENV serotypes (especially DENV-3 reemergence alongside DENV-1) were reported in Brazil in early 2024; serotype data is supplementary but may appear in official reports.

LANGUAGE — Primary official sources will be in Brazilian Portuguese. Query terms and extraction logic must accommodate Portuguese-language field labels (e.g., 'casos prováveis', 'óbitos', 'internações', 'semana epidemiológica').

GEOGRAPHIC GRANULARITY — Brazil has 26 states + 1 federal district and 5,570 municipalities. Subnational_location should capture state (UF) at minimum; locality should capture municipality where reported. Do not aggregate state figures into national totals without flagging.
TIME GRANULARITY — Q1 2024 corresponds to Epidemiological Weeks SE01–SE13 (approximately January 1 – March 30, 2024). Map SE numbers to calendar date ranges when populating date_reported.
DATA LAG — SINAN-based official counts may be subject to reporting delays of 1–4 weeks; boletim closing dates should be recorded in evidence_quote or notes.

CASE CLASSIFICATION — Brazilian dengue surveillance classifies cases as: (1) dengue sem sinais de alarme, (2) dengue com sinais de alarme, (3) dengue grave. Map these to cases_confirmed / cases_probable / cases_suspected fields with a classification note.

DO NOT INVENT URLs — This profile provides source planning intelligence only. No URLs have been discovered or validated. Source URLs must be obtained through actual source discovery and collection steps.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify primary Brazilian Ministry of Health (Ministério da Saúde / SVSA) epidemiological bulletins and situation reports for Dengue in Brazil covering 2024-01-01 to 2024-03-31, with subnational breakdowns by state (UF) and municipality.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: The Brazilian Ministry of Health (MS/SVSA) publishes weekly and periodic boletins epidemiológicos and informes de dengue that are the authoritative primary source for confirmed, probable, suspected case counts, deaths, and hospitalizations at national and subnational levels.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify state-level health secretariat (Secretarias Estaduais de Saúde – SES) reports for high-burden Brazilian states (e.g., São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, Paraná, Goiás, Bahia, Espírito Santo) covering Q1 2024 dengue data.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: SES reports provide subnational and municipal-level granularity not always available in national bulletins, and are critical for locality-level fields.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify PAHO/WHO Dengue situation reports, epidemiological alerts, and regional updates covering Brazil for the period 2024-01-01 to 2024-03-31.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: PAHO publishes dengue situation reports for the Americas that include Brazil-specific case and death counts, often with epidemiological week breakdowns useful for date alignment.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify independent structured databases or dashboards (e.g., InfoDengue, SINAN open data, Brasil.io, DATASUS) containing dengue surveillance data for Brazil in Q1 2024 for cross-validation of collected records.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Structured databases provide independently queryable case counts that can be compared against extracted records from official bulletins to detect discrepancies in count semantics (cumulative vs. weekly) or geographic scope.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify WHO Disease Outbreak News (DON) or ECDC rapid risk assessments referencing the Brazil 2024 dengue epidemic for independent validation of national-level totals.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: WHO DONs and ECDC assessments aggregate data from multiple official sources and serve as independent validation anchors for national case and death totals.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify sources explaining Brazilian dengue case definitions (dengue sem sinais de alarme, dengue com sinais de alarme, dengue grave), classification criteria, and reporting methodology used in 2024 surveillance.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Understanding case classification is essential for correctly mapping extracted counts to schema fields (cases_confirmed, cases_probable, cases_suspected) and interpreting evidence quotes.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify peer-reviewed literature or preprints describing the 2024 Brazil dengue epidemic epidemiology, serotype distribution (DENV-1/2/3/4), and outbreak dynamics for contextual interpretation.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Literature sources provide methodological context, case definition clarifications, and serotype data that support accurate extraction and normalization of surveillance records.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Identify reputable news and situation reports (Reuters, AP, BBC, G1/Globo, Agência Brasil, ProMED) covering the Brazil 2024 dengue outbreak with specific case/death figures and subnational locations.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: News reports may surface early outbreak signals, municipal-level data, or emergency declarations with extractable numeric counts not yet reflected in official bulletins.

source_discovery_objectives.objective: Flag sources with ambiguous count semantics (cumulative vs. weekly vs. newly reported), unclear geographic scope, or potential validation leakage for human review before extraction.
source_discovery_objectives.rationale: Brazil's 2024 dengue epidemic generated very high case volumes; sources may mix cumulative annual totals with weekly increments, requiring human judgment on count type assignment.

planned_source_categories.why_relevant: Ministério da Saúde do Brasil / Secretaria de Vigilância em Saúde e Ambiente (SVSA) publishes authoritative weekly boletins epidemiológicos de dengue and informes de arboviroses covering national and state-level case counts, deaths, hospitalizations, and epidemiological week data. Primary collection source for all target fields.

State health secretariats (SES) of high-burden states (São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, Paraná, Goiás, Bahia, Espírito Santo, Rio Grande do Sul) publish state-specific dengue bulletins with municipal-level breakdowns, enabling subnational_location and locality field population.

PAHO/OPAS publishes dengue situation reports for the Americas with Brazil-specific case and death counts, epidemiological week breakdowns, and serotype data. Serves as both collection and validation source.
WHO Disease Outbreak News and ECDC rapid risk assessments provide independently compiled national-level dengue totals for Brazil that can validate extracted records from primary sources.

Structured surveillance databases including InfoDengue (Fiocruz), SINAN open data (DATASUS), and Brasil.io provide queryable dengue case data at state and municipal levels for Q1 2024, enabling systematic validation of extracted records.

Peer-reviewed studies and preprints on the 2024 Brazil dengue epidemic provide case definitions, serotype distribution, outbreak dynamics, and epidemiological context for accurate extraction and normalization.

Reputable Brazilian and international news outlets (G1/Globo, Agência Brasil, Reuters, ProMED) and situation reports may contain early outbreak signals, municipal-level data, and emergency declarations with extractable numeric counts.

selection_manifest.human_review_reason:
G1 (g1.globo.com) is the digital news portal of Grupo Globo, Brazil's largest and most established media conglomerate. While it is unambiguously a secondary/media source and not an official public health authority, it occupies a meaningfully different position than a generic or low-reputation news outlet. Several factors warrant a modest upward advisory adjustment from the deterministic "low" rating:

1. PUBLISHER IDENTITY: The missing `publisher` field in metadata is a pipeline gap, not a genuine ambiguity. G1/Globo is a nationally recognized, editorially accountable Brazilian broadcaster with a long track record of health reporting. The deterministic penalty for `missing_publisher` is technically correct but overstates actual uncertainty here.

2. PROVENANCE SIGNAL: The article title explicitly cites a national cumulative figure (>1 million cases, 214 deaths) with a precise date (2024-02-29), consistent with the known epidemic context (Brazil declared a public health emergency in February 2024). G1 health reporting at this scale routinely cites Ministério da Saúde / SVSA boletins as primary sources. The provenance_score of 0.85 reflects this.

3. ROLE APPROPRIATENESS: The deterministic role of "context" is appropriate and should be retained. This source should NOT be used as a primary data source for case counts. However, it can serve as a corroborating context signal and — critically — as a pointer to the underlying official source (MS/SVSA boletim) that should be the actual collection target.

4. GEOGRAPHIC GRANULARITY CONCERN: The title and snippet suggest national-level aggregates only. The collection spec requires subnational_location (state/UF) and locality (municipality). This source is unlikely to provide the required geographic granularity for direct extraction. This is the most significant practical limitation.

5. SCREENING/CRITIC DISAGREEMENT FLAG: The `screening_and_critic_disagree` risk flag is notable and warrants human review. This flag suggests internal pipeline tension that has not been resolved deterministically.

6. INDEPENDENCE CONCERN: G1 is an independent media outlet, but its health data is derivative of official sources. The independence_score of 0.42 is reasonable; the source should not be treated as an independent data point from official MS figures it likely cites.

7. PIPELINE WARNINGS: Two active pipeline warnings (`extraction_record_model_still_hantavirus_named`, `source_discovery_not_yet_disease_generic`) indicate upstream schema and discovery risks that could affect how data from this source is mapped, regardless of source quality. These must be resolved before any extraction attempt.

This source (techdengue.com) presents several compounding credibility concerns for a public health data collection task. The domain name is thematically branded ("techdengue") but has no identified publisher, no institutional affiliation, and no verifiable editorial authority. The deterministic assessment already penalizes it heavily (credibility_score=0.357, risk_penalty=0.26), and the LLM advisory concurs. While disease relevance and timeliness are strong (0.95 each), these are surface-level signals — the title and URL clearly reference dengue Brazil 2024-2025, but topical alignment does not substitute for authoritative provenance. The authority score (0.48) is below threshold for a primary collection source, and the independence score (0.42) raises concerns about whether the content is original analysis or an aggregation/repackaging of official data without clear attribution. The geographic granularity score (0.25) and local relevance score (0.25) suggest the source may not provide the subnational (state/municipality) resolution required by the collection spec. The missing publisher field is a significant red flag in a public health epidemiological context where source traceability is mandatory. The 'screening_and_critic_disagree' flag warrants LLM-layer scrutiny. The deterministic layer did not recommend human review, but given the combination of missing publisher, low authority, independence ambiguity, and the high-stakes epidemiological context (Brazil's declared public health emergency, Q1 2024), the LLM advisory layer upgrades this to human review recommended. This source should not be used as a primary data source. If content is accessed and found to cite official Brazilian sources (MS, SVSA, SES boletins), those upstream sources should be pursued directly instead.

This source is a ResearchGate-hosted publication titled "Epidemia de Dengue: uma análise sobre as projeções para o ano de 2024." Several compounding factors reduce its suitability for primary epidemiological data collection:

1. **Platform identity mismatch**: ResearchGate is a preprint/academic social networking platform, not a peer-reviewed journal or official public health repository. Publications hosted there may be preprints, conference papers, or author self-deposits without formal peer review. The source_type tag of "news_and_situation_report" is a mismatch — this is more accurately an academic/grey-literature document, which further complicates role assignment.

2. **Projection-focused framing**: The title explicitly references "projeções" (projections/forecasts) for 2024, not confirmed surveillance counts. This is a critical semantic distinction for a task requiring confirmed case counts, deaths, hospitalizations, and subnational breakdowns from Q1 2024. Projection data cannot be substituted for observed surveillance data in the required fields.

3. **Missing publisher metadata**: No publisher is recorded. For a ResearchGate document, this means the originating journal, institution, or authoring body is unverifiable from metadata alone, raising provenance concerns.

4. **Low local relevance score (0.25)**: Geographic granularity is unclear. A projection analysis may aggregate at the national level or use modeled estimates rather than state/municipality-level observed counts, which are required by the collection spec (subnational_location, locality).

5. **Independence unclear (0.42)**: The authorship and institutional affiliation are unknown from metadata, making it impossible to assess whether this is an independent academic analysis or a derivative of official data without proper attribution.

6. **Screening/critic disagreement flag**: The "screening_and_critic_disagree" risk flag is notable — it suggests internal pipeline tension about this source's role, warranting advisory caution.

7. **No data signal in source metadata**: source_disease_relevance_data_signal_count = 0, meaning no structured data fields (case counts, deaths, etc.) were detected in the metadata. The document may discuss dengue epidemiology conceptually without providing extractable surveillance records.

8. **Role hint vs. actual utility**: The role_hint of "collection_support" and the deterministic role of "context" are consistent. This source may be useful for understanding the epidemic framing or corroborating narrative context, but should not be used as a primary data source for case/death counts.

**Summary**: This source is appropriately rated low credibility for primary data collection purposes. It may serve a narrow contextual role (e.g., confirming that a 2024 dengue epidemic was recognized in the literature), but its projection-based framing, platform ambiguity, missing publisher, and absence of detected data signals make it unsuitable for populating required surveillance fields.

This source is a YouTube video discovered via live search, with no publisher metadata, no structured data, and no verifiable authorship chain. While the title references a specific and plausible cumulative case figure (715,000 dengue cases in Brazil in 2024) that aligns with the known epidemic context — including Brazil's February 2024 public health emergency declaration — the platform (youtube.com) is a video-sharing host, not a public health authority or journalistic outlet with editorial accountability. The deterministic assessment correctly assigns low credibility (0.357) and a 'context' role. Key concerns include: (1) the publisher field is null, making it impossible to assess the originating news organization or official body behind the video; (2) YouTube as a domain carries no inherent editorial or epidemiological authority; (3) geographic granularity is low (0.25/0.30), meaning the source likely reports only national-level aggregates, insufficient for subnational field population; (4) independence is unclear (0.42), raising the possibility of secondary or tertiary reporting; (5) the 'screening_and_critic_disagree' flag warrants attention — if any upstream screening step rated this source higher, that disagreement should be resolved before use. The disease relevance is high (0.95) and timeliness is strong (0.95), confirming topical alignment, but these do not compensate for structural credibility deficits. The source may serve as a corroborating signal or lead to an identifiable primary source (e.g., a Ministério da Saúde boletim cited within the video), but should not be used as a primary or direct collection source. Human review is advisable specifically to resolve the screener-critic disagreement flag and to determine whether the video credits a primary official source that could be independently retrieved.

metric_row_extraction_audit.row_quote: ![Brand](https://www.cofen.gov.br/wp-content/themes/cofen/assets/imagens/logo-cofen.png) ![Transparência e Prestação de Contas](https://www.cofen.gov.br/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/transp_logo-1.png) ###### Transparência e Prestação de Contas ### Dengue aumentou 400% no Brasil em 2024 em comparação ao ano passado ##### Apesar de uma queda recente nos casos, especialistas alertam que a doença voltará a crescer em dezembro 18.10.2024 ![Mosquito Aedes aegypti. Feche um Mosquito sugando sangue humano](https://www.cofen.gov.br/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/mosquito-aedes-aegypti-feche-um-mosquito-sugando-sangue-humano_45334-157.avif) O Brasil registrou 6,5 milhões de casos prováveis de dengue até 7 de outubro de 2024, de acordo com o [Painel de Monitoramento das Arboviroses](https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/a/aedes-aegypti/monitoramento-das-arboviroses) do Ministério da Saúde. O coeficiente de incidência é de 3.221,7 por 100 mil habitantes, enquanto a Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS) considera que taxas acima de 300 por 100 mil já indicam epidemia. No período, 5.536 pessoas morreram em decorrência da dengue, e outros 1.591 óbitos estão em investigação. Para efeito de comparação, no mesmo período de 2023, foram registrados 1,3 milhão de casos prováveis da doença, com 1.179 mortes confirmadas ao longo do ano. O aumento de casos em 2024 é 400% maior em relação ao ano anterior. Apesar desses números alarmantes, as infecções começaram a cair a partir de abril. A redução se manteve até o final de agosto, mas especialistas alertam para uma possível nova alta em dezembro, com expectativa de pico entre março e abril de 2025. O estado de São Paulo concentra 32,3% dos casos, totalizando 2,1 milhões de infecções e 1.786 mortes.
